Based on the uploaded Machine Learning session transcript dated 11/8/2026. The session covers linear
regression cost function, ordinary least squares (OLS), gradient descent, learning rate, parameter updates,
convergence, MSE/RMSE/R², and a house-price example. 1. Linear Regression: Finding the Best-Fit Line
Linear regression may have many possible lines near the observed data. The key question is how to decide which
line is the best fit. The lecture defines the best-fit line as the line having minimum error or residual. Best-Fit Line → Minimum Error
2. Linear Regression Equation
ŷ = β₀ + β₁x
y = mx + c
• β₀ / c → intercept
• β₁ / m → slope/coefficient
• x → independent variable
• y → actual target
• ŷ → predicted target
The objective is to find the coefficients that minimize the cost. 3. Error / Residual
The error is the difference between predicted and actual values.

Error / Residual
The error is the difference between predicted and actual values. The lecture uses squared error so that errors are
measured through their squared magnitude. Error = ŷ − y
Squared Error = (ŷ − y)²
The sum of squared errors is referred to as SSE. 4. Cost Function
For linear regression, the lecture uses Mean Squared Error (MSE) as the cost function. The cost function is
denoted by J and depends on β₀ and β₁. J(β₀, β₁) = (1/n) Σ(ŷᵢ − yᵢ)²
J = MSE
Machine Learning — Linear Regression Notes

The goal is to minimize J. Zero error is generally not realistic for real-world data, so we seek the minimum possible
error. L22-L30
5. Two Methods for Minimizing Cost
• Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
• Gradient Descent
OLS is presented as a direct/closed-form method. Gradient descent is presented as an iterative optimization
method. 6. Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)
OLS calculates the regression coefficients directly using standard formulas. It does not require iterative
parameter initialization and updating in the way gradient descent does. OLS → Closed-Form / Direct
Gradient Descent → Iterative
OLS obtains the standard coefficient formulas by taking derivatives of the cost function with respect to the
coefficients and setting those derivatives equal to zero. 7. Why Set Derivatives to Zero? To minimize J, OLS takes the partial derivatives with respect to β₀ and β₁ and equates them to zero. ∂J/∂β₀ = 0
∂J/∂β₁ = 0
Solving these equations gives the standard OLS formulas. 8.

8. OLS Slope Formula
β₁ = Σ[(xᵢ − ̄x)(yᵢ − ȳ)] / Σ[(xᵢ − ̄x)²]
• xᵢ → individual x value
• yᵢ → individual y value
• ̄x → mean of x
• ȳ → mean of y
The lecture explains that this formula comes from differentiating the cost function and setting the derivative to
zero. 9. OLS Intercept Formula
β₀ = ȳ − β₁̄x
Once β₁, ̄x and ȳ are known, the intercept can be calculated directly. Machine Learning — Linear Regression Notes

10. Derivative — Basic Meaning
The lecture gives an intuitive definition: a derivative represents the rate of change of one quantity with respect to
another. Derivative → Rate of Change
Because J depends on both β₀ and β₁, partial derivatives are used. ∂J/∂β₀ → Rate of change of J with respect to β₀
∂J/∂β₁ → Rate of change of J with respect to β₁
A detailed calculus derivation is intentionally outside this session's scope. 11. Loss Function vs Cost Function
The lecture distinguishes the terminology based on the amount of data being considered:
Loss Function → Error for a single data point
Cost Function → Aggregate error over the dataset
The transcript notes that the formulas are essentially the same in the discussed context; the terminology differs
by usage. 12. Why We Need Gradient Descent
OLS is useful because it directly calculates the coefficients, but the lecture points out that when the real dataset
has thousands or millions of variables, the computation can become very time-consuming.

has thousands or millions of variables, the computation can become very time-consuming. OLS is therefore

not limited to linear regression; it can be used in other machine-learning models as well. Gradient Descent → Minimize J

2. Find the downhill direction

3. Take a small step using α
4. Repeat until reaching/converging near the minimum
The lecture describes these steps as repeating until the minimum of the cost function is reached. 15. Parameter Initialization
The initial values of β₀ and β₁ can be random. Zero is also possible; it is not mandatory that the values be zero. The

The lecture describes the cost function as convex. In a 2D visualization it looks like a parabola; with multiple

The objective is to reach the minimum point. The lecture connects a single minimum with the discussed no-

The learning rate α controls the size of the step taken during each parameter update. It is a hyperparameter
selected before training. α = Learning Rate = Step Size
The lecture gives 0.01 and 0.001 as example values. 19. Effect of Learning Rate

The instructor uses these two cases to explain why learning-rate selection matters. 20. Gradient Descent Update Rule
β₁(new) = β₁(old) − α(∂J/∂β₁)
β₀(new) = β₀(old) − α(∂J/∂β₀)
The gradient is calculated for each parameter and the parameters are updated repeatedly. 21. Why the Negative Sign? This is one of the lecture's key concepts. The derivative/gradient indicates the direction of increasing cost. Since
gradient descent wants to decrease cost, it moves in the opposite direction. Gradient → Increasing Cost Direction
−Gradient → Decreasing Cost Direction
The negative sign therefore guides the parameters toward the minimum. 22. Starting From the Left Side
On the left side of the convex curve, the slope is negative. In the update rule, subtracting a negative gradient

βnew < βold
Thus, either starting side eventually directs the parameter toward the minimum. 24. Convergence
Convergence means that the cost function has reached a point where further iterations no longer produce
meaningful decreases. Cost decreases → Cost stabilizes → Convergence

When α is too large, each update can be so large that the algorithm jumps across the minimum rather than
